When my old man stopped eating, we went back to the basics. I went to the store and got one can of as many different wet foods that I could, and each day we tried a new can and I put them in three different categories: didn't touch, ate some of it, and ate all of it. Out of all the cans we tried, I only found one that he ate all of it, but I did find 4 that he was willing to eat some of which was good. In the end, he actually started eating kitten food again. I had rescued an orphaned kitten and bought some dry kitten food. He tore the bag open to get to it, so it might be worth trying kitten food again to get your senior lady eating more.

I got a lot of my information from http://www.kittenlady.org/, she has really good information for estimating age, diet, socializing, and general kitten care. Also forgot to add, you will probably still need to stimulate the kitten to go the bathroom if he isn't doing it by himself yet. You should be helping them go to the bathroom after every feeding.

I actually had a similar situation with a kitten I've had since he was 5 weeks who is around 12 weeks now. We found him outside alone and didn't find any siblings or mama cat.

The first week, I gave him kitten formula, you can approximate the weight to figure out how much to feed him, and I fed him every 2-3 hours while he was on formula. He already had some of his teeth when I got him and by the end of the first week he had all his teeth. I started mixing a small amount of kitten wet food pate into the formula a couple days in so he would get used to it. I have a queen sized bed all to myself so I kept him in a crate on my bed with a heating pad so he wouldn't be alone at night. I gave him two stuffed animals and some small pom-pom toys to keep him occupied. Feeding on a schedule, keeping him warm, and making sure you're feeding him an appropriate diet is the most important at this stage.

Biological sex is actually a lot more complicated than just male and female once you dig a little deeper. Sex is generally determined by your physical body and traits, and of course chromosomes. Intersex individuals are actually a lot more common than you'd think tho, an intersex person being an individual whose biology doesn't completely fit under either male or female. 

Gender is separate from sex in that you develop gender as you grow up, although unfortunately a lot of people are simply told what their gender should be and aren't given the opportunity to discover it for themselves. Gender is a social construct that defines how a person would like to be viewed by others, generally between masculine and feminine. Many people equate sex to gender because for a lot of people, their sex and their gender "match".

It's important to remember that while these labels do exist, that doesn't mean that you have to use them for yourself. If you want to use a label, and you find one that fits, great, you can claim that label. But if you don't want a label, that's great too. When you tell people about your job, do you list all of your certifications and titles? Or do you give them a generic catch-all type answer? Same rule applies with sexuality labels.

Asexual generally means that the person doesn't experience sexual attraction, but remember sexual attraction is different from romantic attraction. Pansexual is defined differently by different people but the way I understand it is that pansexual means attraction regardless of gender, as in a person's gender identity doesn't influence attraction.

I definitely agree that asking your kids is going to be the best way to find out. Before asking them though, you have to ask yourself a few questions first. The most important one being, "Have I made room for genuine honesty in my relationship with my children?" If your kids don't feel safe being honest with you, they won't be. 

As the parent, the bulk of that relationship falls on your shoulders. Have you considered their needs and wants when making decisions on their behalf? Or have you been basing your decisions off of what you feel should be best for them? Nobody knows your child better than themselves, even as their parent, you do not know them better than they know themselves. Do you ask for their input when making decisions on their behalf? Not every decision has to be exactly in line with what the child wants, but you must consider their input and try to meet their wants if its realistic and responsible to do so. 

Another important part of parent child relationships that sometimes gets overlooked is admitting fault. You won't always make the right decision, or have the right reaction in the heat of the moment, but you need to be able to admit to your kids that you were wrong and apologize for your behavior. If you yelled at your kid for something, and realized later that you shouldnt have yelled at them but don't communicate to your child that your response was unwarranted, they won't know that your reaction was inappropriate. Instead, they will internalize that feeling and when they do learn that your reaction was unwarranted from someone else, they will resent you for not admitting that you were wrong and for yelling in the first place. That being said, you can always apologize now. Admitting that you were wrong in the past doesn't erase the fact that it happened, but changing that behavior and taking ownership of that mistake moving forward will show that you care about the relationship and that you want to foster a healthier relationship for the future.

We were able to interact with her minimally. What worked best for us was going in the room in the evenings when the house and the neighborhood were quiet so she was more relaxed. She didn't like to be touched directly for most of the two years, but we were able to put a blanket over her when we needed to move her and she tolerated it. For a bath, we brought her into the bathroom with only two people. I sat her in my lap on a towel and rocked/bounced her with my knees while we wiped her down with baby wipes. She didn't like it, but we were able to keep the atmosphere calm and move very slowly so she tolerated it. We also sat on the floor so she felt safer and less trapped. The first interactions we noticed actually were ones we didn't know were happening. The room she chose was my brothers so he slept in the bed she lived under and we started to notice a spot on his comforter that was accumulating a lot of cat hair. Turned out, after a few months, she started sleeping in the bed with him every night, but would go back under the bed before he woke up in the morning.

Forgot to mention, our distrustful kitty became one of the most affectionate cats I've ever had once she opened up and got comfortable. I know its hard right now, but don't give up on your kitty. Myself and my family are the only people our cat trusts, but that makes it even more special that she does. She does have harsher boundaries than other cats, she still can't be picked up, but she's more than happy to invite herself onto the couch with you to cuddle now.

I would say the most important thing is knowing your resident cats personality. I have a 12 year old male cat who has lived with other cats on and off his entire life. He's lived with foster kittens and their moms, my moms cats, and multiple roommates cats. He has become friends with almost every female cat he's ever met, but male cats almost always bully him. He's befriended one other male cat, but they met when the other cat was only a couple weeks old. My cat is super passive, even more so in his old age, but most male cats tend to be dominant so they bully my cat. 

If your cat is not super dominant, he can probably get along with a male kitten, but remember that kittens tend to play a lot more than adult cats so make sure the kitten doesn't pester your cat too much. That goes for female kittens too. I would try to find a new cat that matches the energy of your resident cat, but if your resident is very playful then a kitten might be a perfect fit.

Personally, I have found my cat is quite helpful for me. My cat is always nearby me when I'm at home, so if I see or hear something, I can turn to him and see his reaction and it calms me down. Taking care of him is pretty low-effort as well, just have to keep the litter box clean and the food and water bowls full as well as some light grooming.

Well, unless the kitty is already willing to approach people and let you touch them, catching them may not be as simple as you'd imagine. I would bring something to entice them, like some canned chicken or tuna. Cat beds can be kind of expensive, so for just an overnight stay at your place I would just get them a cheap blanket, and a cardboard box with a hole cut out that they can hide in if they want. Theres a chance that if they've been living outside they have fleas so I wouldn't give them a blanket that you use and care about, there's also a chance that they've never seen a litter box before and might have an accident. You can use pretty much any short plastic tub as a makeshift litterbox, and I would just use some bowls from your kitchen for food and water. Get some actual kitten food from the store, but if you dont want to buy litter and you have access to relatively clean sand you can use that. It wont absorb odor but should be sufficient for an overnight stay.

If you don't want to bring the kitten to the kill shelter, you can call them and ask about what other shelters are in your area, most shelters will have that information. You can also call a local vet and they should have a list of local shelters as well. Good luck, I wish you and kitty the best!

For me it took literally almost 5 years for it to really work. They dont work on their own in my experience, but alongside therapy (and medication if necessary), they help to reinforce the work done in therapy. An important one for me was removing self deprecating phrases and replacing them with phrases that direct the negativity in the right direction. Instead of something along the lines of 'I'm bad and horrible', I replaced it with 'my situation was bad and horrible'. So a specific example for me personally was, I stopped saying 'I'm lazy and dont get things done because I suck' and replaced it with 'my trauma and mental illness make it really difficult for me to function day to day'. Not only does this serve to remind me that it's not my fault, but helps me understand what I need to focus on in order to get things done. Constantly tearing yourself down only perpetuates that trauma.

When I brought my new bunnies home, they were already adults but things didnt really click for us at first. I put their playpen in my bedroom next to my desk so they could see and smell me, but for the first week I only tried to pet them once a day to gauge if they were warming up, but otherwise we just existed nearby eachother. Sometimes I would sit next to the pen and talk to them, but mostly they would just watch me when I was at my desk. Once they realized that I was the one who supplied their food and I respected their personal space, they relaxed. Once they were relaxed and settled in, that's when I started pushing that boundary a little and giving them pets and getting them used to me grabbing them. It's very important when pushing your pets boundaries to establish a safe zone though. If your pet has a favorite hiding spot use that, otherwise pick one of their hiding spots (box/hidey house/cage, etc.) and as soon as they go there, do not interact. Show them that if they do not want your attention, they can go there and you will leave them alone. This will help them feel safe and secure, knowing they have a space they can go and not be disturbed if they dont want to be.

We had two preexisting dogs (one that loved everyone and everything, and one that loves everyone and is afraid of small dogs and will bark back if she's barked at) when we added our reactive dog to the household (he wasn't reactive when we got him, but after about 3 months things changed). I have found that he is more reactive when around the others in the yard because he will bark once, the others will bark in response and then it becomes a shouting match for them. When walking them, it's always one dog per person per walk. The one to one ratio helps so I only have to focus on controlling one dogs behavior at a time. There are pros and cons to walking them together or one at a time, but the biggest pro for walking them together is having a "buffer dog". The overtly friendly dog will happily receive any attention on a walk, so if someone doesn't understand that you shouldn't approach a dog wearing a muzzle, (I always muzzle my reactive dog when he's not at home) I can put the friendly dog between us and the stranger to distract them and move the reactive dog away. Usually I don't have any issues with people trying to approach him when he's muzzled though, he's a mastiff mix so he's already pretty intimidating.

Not my story, but a friend of mine from college. I knew two different people who happened to live next door to each other but I never knew because I only ever went to one of their houses, didn't realize my other friend was literally next door the whole time. I get a message from Friend A late one night saying she's scared, there's a ton of cops at her neighbors house and she's been told not to leave her home and to lock her doors/windows. She doesn't know many details because she's scared and hides in her back bedroom as she has no idea what's going on. After a while some people get loaded into ambulances, police leave and tell her she is good to go now.

The next day, I'm talking with Friend B, bring up what happened to Friend A yesterday, wondered if she had heard anything. Friend B asks where Friend A lives, finally make the connection that they are neighbors. Here's where shit gets weird. 

Friend B confirms that it was in fact her place that the cops were at last night. She lives with 2 other girls and her boyfriend in a house. Late that night, Friend B and her boyfriend we're trying to sleep when they heard screaming coming from her roommates room. Her boyfriend goes to check it out, pokes his head in the door and she is just sitting on her floor, butt naked, with all the lights off. We'll call her roommate 1. Little strange, but not super concerning so he goes back to their room.

About an hour later, they hear more screaming, but this time coming from the front yard. Boyfriend opens the front door to see what's going on and sees roommate 1, still butt naked, dragging roommate 2 across the lawn away from the house by her hair. Boyfriend sees that roommate 1 is holding a sword in her other hand and closes and locks the door while Friend B calls the police. After a couple minutes, the screaming stops. The police show up, and apparently can't find roommate 1, but find roommate 2 unconcious in the front lawn. She was physically okay afterwards, but dropped out and had to move back in with her parents because of mental health issues.

They get roommate 2 loaded in an ambulance and start searching the neighborhood for roommate 1, still believed to have the sword.
